parts.problem_md:
Fig. 9.1 shows a circuit used in a toy car.

![Circuit diagram with cell P, switch Q, LED S, fixed resistor R, variable resistor T and motor U connected in series, forming a complete electrical circuit.](assets/001-circuit-diagram-with-cell-p-switch-q-led-s-fixed.png)

**Fig. 9.1**

(i) The resistance of component **T** is $5 . 4 Ω$. The resistance of component **U** is $3 . 5 Ω$.

Calculate the combined resistance of components T and U.

[1]

(ii) The current in component R is 2.7 A. The current in component T is 2.5 A.

Determine the current in component S and component U.

[2]

(iii) State the name of component S.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i)

To calculate the combined resistance of components T and U:

$R_{TU} = 5 . 4 + 3 . 5$

$= 8 . 9 Ω$

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - $8 . 9 Ω$ **[1 mark]**

(ii)

Using Kirchhoff's current law at the junction, the current in component R splits between the branch containing S and the branch containing T and U:

$I_{S} = I_{R} - I_{T} = 2 . 7 - 2 . 5$

I<sub>S</sub> = **0.2 A**

Since T and U are in series, the current in U is the same as the current in T:

I<sub>U</sub> = **2.5 A**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - current in S = 0.2 A **[1 mark]**
> - current in U = 2.5 A **[1 mark]**

(iii)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - LED / light-emitting diode **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> At a junction in a circuit, the total current flowing in must equal the total current flowing out (Kirchhoff's current law) — use this to find an unknown branch current when you know the others. Components connected in series (like T and U here) always carry the same current.

parts.problem_md:
Component U is an electric motor. When the motor is switched on, the toy car moves.

(i) Complete Fig. 9.2 to show one energy transfer that occurs.

![Diagram showing energy transfer: from chemical energy in the battery to kinetic energy of the moving car, with an arrow between two labelled boxes.](assets/002-diagram-showing-energy-transfer-from-chemical-en.png)

**Fig. 9.2**

[2]

(ii) The toy car moves for 10 s.

The power input to the motor is 3.6 W.

The useful energy output by the motor is 32 J.

Show that the efficiency of the motor is `89 \%`.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
(i)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - chemical **[1 mark]**
> - kinetic **[1 mark]**

(ii)

To show that the efficiency of the motor is 89%:

- List the known quantities:

- Power input, P = 3.6 W
- Time, t = 10 s
- Useful energy output, = 32 J

- Calculate the useful power output:

$\text{useful power output} = \frac{\text{energy}}{\text{time}} = \frac{32}{10}$ **[1 mark]**

$= 3 . 2 \text{W}$

- Calculate the efficiency:

`\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}} \times 100 \% = \frac{3.2}{3.6} \times 100` **[1 mark]**

= **88.9 \%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for calculating the useful power output as 3.2 W
> 
> - Marks must be awarded in this order
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution into `\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}} \times 100 \%` (accept formula in any form; also accept converting input power to energy first, then using the energy-based efficiency formula)
> 
> 1 mark for a final calculated value of `88.9 \%` shown to at least 3 significant figures

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Show that" questions require you to display your full working, not just a final answer — even if you already know the answer given in the question (89% here), you must show the calculation steps that lead to it to earn the marks.

parts.problem_md:
The student climbs a step into the school.

The student has a mass of 55 kg. The step is 0.15 m high.

Calculate the increase in the gravitational potential energy $\Delta E_{p}$ of the student climbing the step.

Include the unit in your answer.

(Take g = 9.8 N/kg)
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the increase in gravitational potential energy:

- List the known quantities:

- Mass, m = 55 kg
- Height, h = 0.15 m
- Gravitational field strength, g = 9.8 N/kg

- Write down the equation:

$\Delta E_{p} = m g h$

- Substitute the known values:

$\Delta E_{p} = 55 \times 9 . 8 \times 0 . 15$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

∆ E<sub>p</sub> = 80.85 \approx **81** **[1 mark]**

Unit: **J (joules)** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution into $\Delta E_{p} = m g h$ (accept formula in any form)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct answer of 81 J
> 
> - Accept 80.9 or 80.85
> 
> 1 mark for the correct unit, J (joules)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question says "include the unit in your answer", the unit often carries a mark of its own — write J (joules) clearly next to your final number rather than assuming it's understood.

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 7.2 shows a wind turbine used to generate electricity from the power of the wind.

![Simple line drawing of a single wind turbine with three blades on a tall tower, standing on a gently curved ground line](assets/003-simple-line-drawing-of-a-single-wind-turbine-wit.png)

**Fig. 7.2**

A wind turbine produces electrical power of 2200 W at a voltage of 240 V.

Calculate the energy transferred by the wind turbine in 15 seconds.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the energy transferred:

- List the known quantities:

- Power, P = 2200 W
- Time, t = 15 s

- Write down the equation:

$\text{power} = \frac{\text{energy}}{\text{time}}$

- Rearrange for energy:

$E = P \times t$

- Substitute the known values:

$E = 2200 \times 15$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

E = **33 000 J** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution into $E = P \times t$ (accept formula in any form)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of 33 000 J

> **[exam-tip]**
> Watch out for extra information you don't need in the question — the voltage of 240 V isn't required here, since energy transferred depends only on power and time.

parts.problem_md:
The diagram shows a force of 200 N pulling an object up a slope. The object moves 5.0 m along the slope.

The object moves 3.0 m vertically upwards and 4.0 m horizontally.

![Diagram of an object pulled up a 5.0 m inclined plane by a 200 N force, forming a right triangle with 4.0 m base and 3.0 m vertical height](assets/004-diagram-of-an-object-pulled-up-a-5-0-m-inclined-.png)

How much work is done by the 200 N force?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force

$W = F \times d = 200 \times 5 . 0$

$= 1000 \text{J}$

- The distance used is the distance along the slope (5.0 m), not the vertical or horizontal component

**A** is incorrect because 600 J = 200 × 3.0, using the vertical distance instead of the distance along the slope

**B** is incorrect because 800 J = 200 × 4.0, using the horizontal distance instead of the distance along the slope

**D** is incorrect because 1400 J = 200 × 7.0, incorrectly adding the vertical and horizontal distances ($3 . 0 + 4 . 0$) instead of using the distance along the slope
